newsitem.title: HUNGARY: HUNGARY HAS RASH OF BOMBINGS, POLICE SEE CRIME LINK.
newsitem.headline: HUNGARY HAS RASH OF BOMBINGS, POLICE SEE CRIME LINK.

text.p: The third bombing in five days damaged a Budapest nightclub on Wednesday and police blamed crime syndicates for the latest in a spate of blasts which is beginning to rattle residents.
The handgrenade explosion at about 2 a.m. in a section of Budapest frequented by prostitutes caused minor damage to the nightclub and several parked cars, but injured no one, police said.

It was the 26th bombing this year in various parts of Hungary and although police have been at a loss to explain some of the earlier explosions, they said the latest ones appeared to be linked to organised crime.
"Crime syndicates fighting for territory are behind these handgrenade bombings," Laszlo Garamvolgyi, spokesman for the Hungarian National Police, told Reuters.
"These are demonstrations of force by different criminal groups, both foreign and domestic," Garamvolgyi said.
"Police have been working hard on these cases and we expect results in the next few days," he added.

He was referring to the nightclub blast, a blast on Monday that shattered windows of a pizza parlour and an auto showroom, and a bombing on Saturday which wrecked a car belonging to an arcade games operator.
Lieutenant-Colonel Elek Katai of the National Police homicide squad, said the blast near the nightclub "was the 26th bombing this year and only three of those cases have been solved".
The cases "could grow in number", he added, but did not elaborate.
Some of the previous bombings included two apparently aimed at Jewish targets, including a small bomb planted in a dustbin near Budapest's Dohany Utca Synagogue, Europe's largest.
Earlier this month police detained a 17-year-old man who confessed to planting a bomb under a seat in a bus in northern Hungary, which injured four people.
A Slovak man committed suicide with a handgrenade in Budapest this month. Although no other injuries have been reported in the capital, some residents are getting nervous.
"This neighbourhood has turned really bad in the last two years," said Krisztina Petranyi, a young mother who lives with her son in a building across the street from the nightclub.
"Fights on the street happen amost every night...and we try to avoid going out as much as we can," she said.

Another neighbour, Maria Burai, said the early-morning blast "woke everybody up" but police had prevented people from approaching the Crazy Horse nightclub, which earlier had been identified as the White Horse.

Government officials responsible for internal security were not immediately available for comment while Western diplomats said it was too soon to tell if the blasts could have an impact on Hungary's vital tourism industry.
"So far these have been clearly targeted at property and they go out of their way to make sure people are not hurt," a diplomat said.
"It is too soon to know if it is going to have repercussions outside (Hungary)."
